pacing-strategy.short: How an athlete spreads work and energy over a race or effort: when to go hard and when to hold back.

all-out-pacing.short: Going as hard as possible from the start and holding on as speed fades. Suits very short events, about 30 s or less.

positive-pacing.short: Pacing that is fastest early and slows over the race. A 'positive split': the second half takes longer than the first.

negative-pacing.short: Pacing that speeds up over the race. A 'negative split': the second half is faster than the first.

even-pacing.short: Holding the same speed or power from start to finish.

parabolic-pacing.short: A U-, J- or reverse-J-shaped profile: fast start, slower middle, fast finish. In a J the finish is the fastest part, in a reverse J the start.

variable-pacing.short: Speed or power that goes up and down during a race, with hills, wind, corners or rivals' attacks.

end-spurt.short: A rise in speed near the finish of a race. It shows the athlete had kept something in reserve.

feedforward.short: Control set in advance from what is expected, before any feedback arrives. In pacing: the starting pace chosen from the known distance, past races and conditions.

afferent-feedback.short: Information sent to the brain by sensory nerves from the body (muscles, heart, lungs, skin) about what is happening there.

teleoanticipation.short: Regulating pace during exercise from body signals and feelings of effort, with the expected end of the task in mind, so the task is finished within the body's limits.

rpe.short: How hard an effort feels, scored on a scale, most often Borg's 6–20 scale (6 = no exertion, 20 = maximal).

rpe-template.short: The expected rise of RPE over a race of known length, learned from experience: how hard it should feel at each point of the race.

anticipatory-regulation.short: Tucker's model of pacing: the brain sets and adjusts pace ahead of time, using RPE, so that the body's limits are not reached before the finish.

hazard-score.short: De Koning's index: RPE (0–10 scale) × fraction of the race still to go. Below about 1.5 athletes tend to speed up; above about 3 they tend to slow.

psychobiological-model.short: Marcora's model: endurance is limited by a conscious decision, based mainly on perceived effort and motivation, to slow down or stop.

w-prime.short: The fixed amount of work, in kJ, that you can do above critical power before you must slow down. Hard efforts above CP use it up; riding below CP slowly refills it.

w-prime-balance.short: How much of W′ is left at a given moment: it falls whenever power is above critical power and slowly refills when power is below it.

emg.short: Recording the electrical signals of active muscle, here with sensors stuck on the skin. How big and how fast the signals are hints at how many and which motor units are working.

heat-acclimatisation.short: Adapting to heat by training in it repeatedly, mostly within 1–2 weeks: heart rate and core temperature fall and sweating rises, so heat costs less performance.

split-time.short: The time for one section of a race, such as each half of a marathon or each kilometre.

hitting-the-wall.short: A sudden, lasting slowdown late in a marathon, typically after about 32 km, usually because the body's carbohydrate stores run low.

maximal-aerobic-power.short: The highest power reached in a ramp test to VO2max: the power at which the body's top rate of oxygen use is reached. Used as a reference for intensity.

drafting.short: Riding or swimming close behind another athlete, in their slipstream, so the same speed costs less energy. Allowed in elite short-course triathlon, banned in Ironman racing.
